title: From "make me something" to a request you can verify
promise: You'll know how to turn any vague request into a six-piece brief. That brief carries a numbered checklist. You can check it off yourself, just by looking at the screen, with no coding knowledge and in under five minutes.
why: Oscar Benedi runs a bike shop in Zaragoza and gets eleven calls a day booking appointments. He wrote "make me a website for my shop." In two minutes he had a gorgeous website: with a blog and a shopping cart. It even had a catalog of twenty bikes he doesn't sell. It took him three afternoons to understand the problem wasn't the AI. The real problem was something else: he'd never said what needed to come out the other end. He also hadn't said how he'd know if it was right. This lesson is what Oscar should have written on day one. You'll also see how to check in four minutes whether what you got back is usable or should go in the trash.

theory.title: Chatting is free. Briefing costs ten minutes and saves you three afternoons
theory.text: When you chat, you leave gaps. The AI can't leave a gap blank: it fills it with the most likely thing it's seen on the internet. And it fills it well, that's the problem. It gives you back something coherent, orderly, and completely unrelated to your case, and because it's well written, it feels like progress. The doubt coming up right now is this. If the AI understands natural language, why do I have to write like a notary? It understands your words perfectly; what it doesn't have is your head. It doesn't know your customers are over sixty, or that you sell nothing. It also doesn't know that eight out of ten of your bookings come through text, or that you hate long forms. A brief isn't about writing more: it's about writing what only you know.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between two requests to a carpenter. One: "make me a table." The other: "a 180 by 90 table, oak, for six chairs, and it has to fit through a 78-centimeter door." With the first sentence he also makes you a table. With the second he makes you yours, and if it doesn't fit through the door afterward, it's no longer your fault: it's his.
theory.example: Oscar asked for "a website for my bike shop" and got an online store with a shopping cart and a payment gateway. Oscar doesn't sell anything online: he repairs bikes. Eleven words would've been enough: "I don't sell products, I just want people to be able to book a repair." That sentence would have erased 70% of the wasted work before it even started.

theory.title: The six pieces of a brief
theory.text: A complete brief has six pieces and none of them is extra: outcome, context, input and output, boundaries, delivery format, and proof. The outcome is what you want to have at the end, described as a thing, not a task. For example: "a page where the customer books an appointment," not "I want you to work on my website." The context is who's going to use it, from phone or computer, at what moment and in what kind of hurry. Input and output are what reaches the system and exactly what it returns. Boundaries are what it must NOT do, what shouldn't be touched, and what shouldn't be made up. This is the piece that removes half the AI's fabrications before it even starts. The delivery format says whether you want a full file, a list, five sentences, or the complete code with nothing trimmed. And proof, the sixth piece, is how you'll know it's right. It gets its own section in this lesson because it's the one everyone skips. The doubt that always comes up here is the same: do I have to write this every time I open a chat? No: you write it once per project, save it in a text file, and paste it at the start of every new conversation. From the second time on, putting together a brief takes two minutes.
theory.example: Sonia Cabrera runs an accounting firm in a Chicago suburb and gets about 90 emails a day. Her brief, in six pieces. Outcome: a daily inbox summary. Context: she reads it at 8:30 on her phone, standing up, before opening the office. Input: the previous day's emails. Output: a list of at most 15 lines grouped by client. Boundaries: never reply to anyone, never delete anything, never make up deadlines that aren't written in the email. Format: plain text, no tables, readable on a phone screen with no zooming. Proof: seeing that all three of Tuesday's tax-office emails show up. And that no line mentions a date that isn't in the original email.

theory.title: Proof: the piece almost nobody writes
theory.text: Almost everyone writes the first five pieces if you push them a little. Almost nobody writes the sixth, and that's the one that decides whether you're the client or the audience. An acceptance criterion (the sentence that says when something is done) always has the same shape: "if I do X, I see Y." No "works well," "looks professional," or "is fast." Those can't be marked yes or no, and you'll end up arguing with yourself. A valid criterion meets three things. You can check it with your own eyes, it carries a concrete made-up piece of data, and it says what result you expect to see. Each criterion also needs its ugly counterpart. It's not enough to test that it works when everything goes right. You need to test what happens when the customer leaves the name field blank or types a five-digit phone number. And the most important part: this list gets written BEFORE anything is built. If you write it afterward, you'll write it looking at what's already in front of you and approve whatever, because that's how we are.
theory.example: Bad criterion: "the form should work." Good criterion: "If I type Oscar Benedi / 555-111-2222 / rear tire change and click Submit, I see a green message that says Appointment requested and an email arrives at shop@wheellibre.com in under a minute." Its ugly counterpart: "If I leave the phone field blank and click Submit, nothing gets sent, red text appears below the phone field, and whatever I'd already typed stays there without being erased."

theory.title: Before and after, the same request
theory.text: This is literally the same thing Oscar wanted, written two ways. The before version has fourteen words and sounds reasonable. The after version has about two hundred thirty and takes eight minutes to write. With the first, Oscar got back four hundred lines of code. He had no way of knowing if it was right or wrong other than reading it, which he doesn't know how to do. With the second he opened the page and ran his six checks in four minutes, phone in hand. Three passed and three didn't, and he answered with one sentence: "Criteria 2, 4, and 6 fail. Fix them without touching anything else." The difference isn't in the AI's quality, which was the same. It's that the second time, Oscar could say no.
theory.example:
BEFORE (14 words):
"Make me a website for my bike shop, modern and professional looking."

AFTER:
"I want a single-screen website for Wheel Libre, a bike repair shop in Zaragoza. I do NOT sell anything online: I only repair. The page's single goal is for the customer to book an appointment without calling me.

Who uses it: people 30 to 65, seven out of ten on mobile, many in a hurry and standing on the street.

What comes in and what goes out: the customer types their name, phone number, and picks one of these three services: tune-up $25, tire change $45, full inspection $90. On submit, they see a confirmation message on screen and I get an email at shop@wheellibre.com with those three details plus the date and time of the request.

Boundaries: no shopping cart, no payments, no blog, no product catalog, no user accounts or passwords. Don't make up prices, hours, address, or phone number: if you're missing data, leave it written as MISSING DATA and ask me.

Delivery format: a single complete HTML file, no trimming and no '...unchanged from here...', that I can open by double-clicking. Explain in three lines where I need to edit if I want to change the prices.

How I'll check it:
1. I open the file on my phone and read Wheel Libre and the three services with their prices without zooming.
2. I type Oscar / 555-111-2222 / tune-up and click Submit: I see a confirmation message on screen.
3. I leave the phone field blank and click Submit: nothing gets sent and a red warning appears below the field.
4. I type a 5-digit phone number and click Submit: nothing gets sent and I get warned.
5. Nowhere on the page do the words buy, cart, or bike price appear.
6. I click Submit twice in a row and it doesn't create two requests."

theory.title: A brief gets read aloud before you sign off on it
theory.text: Once the brief is written, don't launch it yet: ask for the echo first. The echo is the AI handing your brief back to you in its own words. You also ask it to tell you what it's assuming and to ask you what it's missing. Two good things happen: you catch misunderstandings while they're still free, and you get a list of decisions you hadn't made. And here's the usual doubt: what if it asks me ten questions I can't answer? That's the best possible outcome. Those ten questions are ten decisions someone was going to make anyway. Either you make them now in five minutes, or it makes them on its own and you find out the day after tomorrow. The rule when reading the echo is harsh and simple. If what it gives back doesn't match what you had in your head, the brief is broken, not the AI. Find the piece that failed, rewrite it, and ask for the echo again. It costs ninety seconds and it's the cheapest thing you'll do in the whole project.
theory.example: Sonia asked for the echo on her email summary. The first question was: "What do I do with an email that has an attachment? Summarize it, ignore it, or flag that there's an attachment?" Sonia had never thought about that, and it turns out four out of ten of her emails have an attachment. She answered in twenty seconds and saved herself a useless daily summary.

theory.title: The right size: whatever fits a five-minute check
theory.text: A brief with twenty acceptance criteria isn't a brief, it's four disguised as one. And when you ask for all four at once, the AI does all four halfway. Then you don't know which one broke what worked yesterday. The practical rule: if your list goes past eight criteria, stop and cut it. The doubt is always the same: but I want the whole website, not a lone form. You'll get it, and you'll get it sooner by splitting it up. First, the page looks right on mobile with your details. Then, the form collects data and confirms. Then, hours and the vacation notice. Each piece gets checked and closed before the next one opens. The hidden reward arrives the day something breaks. You'll know exactly which brief broke it, because the previous one you approved with your own list in hand and your own eyes. Fixing a small brief you just closed is a five-minute conversation. Fixing a huge one from two weeks ago is starting from zero.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between two ways of having your apartment painted. One: the painter does the whole thing and hands you the bill at the end. The other: you order it room by room, and you walk in to check each one before the next starts. In the second case, if the living room blue isn't your blue, you've lost one room. In the first, you've lost the apartment.

tasks.title: Write your weak request, exactly as it comes out
tasks.where: In Windows Notepad, your phone's Notes app, or on paper. Outside the AI.
tasks.action: Before learning anything, put on record where you were about to start. Write in a single line what you would have asked ChatGPT or Claude today about your idea. Do it in your own words and don't clean it up. "Make me a website for my business" works, "I want an assistant to organize my work" works. Don't delete or improve it: you'll need it in task 6 to compare. Save the file as brief.txt on your Desktop. This is where all of this lesson's pieces will end up living.
tasks.expect: A brief.txt file on your Desktop with a single sentence in it, yours, written exactly as it came out.
tasks.stuck: If you can't even manage the weak sentence, the idea doesn't exist outside your head yet. Write this other one instead: "I want something that does ___ and uses ___." Fill in both blanks with the first thing that comes to mind. That's enough to get started.

tasks.title: Let the AI interview you to pull out the six pieces
tasks.where: In the Claude app (claude.ai) or ChatGPT (chatgpt.com), in a new chat.
tasks.action: Open the app and click the new chat button. In Claude it's the pencil-and-paper icon top left. In ChatGPT it says "New chat" in the same spot. Starting clean matters: if you continue in an old chat, you drag along things you said a week ago and won't know what it's actually using. Copy the prompt below, fill in the two bracketed blanks with your details, and send it. Then answer its questions one at a time, without jumping ahead. This will take five to ten minutes, and it'll be the best-spent time in the lesson.
tasks.prompt:
Act as a project manager who works with clients who can't code and is sick of getting vague requests. Your job today is NOT to build anything or propose solutions: it's to pull a complete brief out of my head.

What I would have asked an AI, exactly as it came out: [PASTE YOUR WEAK SENTENCE HERE]
What I do and who's going to use this: [YOUR WORK AND WHO'LL USE IT]

A complete brief has six pieces and I'm missing almost all of them:
1. OUTCOME: what I want to have at the end, described as a thing, not a task.
2. CONTEXT: who uses it, from where (mobile or computer), at what moment, what they know and don't know.
3. INPUT AND OUTPUT: what reaches the system and exactly what it returns.
4. BOUNDARIES: what it must NOT do, what shouldn't be touched, what shouldn't be made up.
5. DELIVERY FORMAT: what you need to hand back to me and in what form.
6. PROOF: how I'll know, just by looking at the screen with no coding knowledge, that it's right.

Interview rules, follow them strictly:
- Ask me ONE question per message and wait for my answer. Never several at once.
- Maximum three lines per question, in plain language. Translate any technical word in parentheses the first time you use it.
- Below each question give me three example answers, so I understand what you're asking. I can pick one or write my own.
- If I answer something vague ("the usual," "it depends," "looking good"), don't accept it: push back and ask for a concrete case or a number.
- Don't propose technologies, tools, design, or code until we're done.
- When you have all six pieces complete, and only then, write me the whole brief as a single block of text I can copy and save.

Start with question 1.
tasks.expect: A single short question on screen, with three example answers below it. If it dumps ten questions at once or starts proposing tools, it didn't read the rules.
tasks.stuck: If it answers with a wall of text or skips its turn, write: "You skipped the one-question-per-message rule. Start over from question 1." If it asks you something you can't answer, reply "I don't know, decide it yourself and note it as an assumption." That's a legitimate answer and it'll show up in task 4's echo.

tasks.title: Ask for the checklist before anything gets built
tasks.where: In the same chat, right after it hands you the complete brief.
tasks.action: When the interview ends, the AI will give you the brief as one block. Copy it and paste it into your brief.txt Desktop file before continuing, in case it gets lost. Now comes the piece almost nobody writes. Send the prompt below, pasting your brief inside it. What it gives back is the list you'll use to accept or reject the work. You have it in hand before a single line of anything exists. Save it too in brief.txt, below the brief.
tasks.prompt:
Here's my finished brief:

[PASTE YOUR COMPLETE BRIEF HERE]

Don't build anything yet. First I want the checklist I'll use to accept or reject your work.

Write me 5 to 8 acceptance criteria. Rules for each one:
- Mandatory form: "If I do [specific action with specific data], I see [specific result]." Banned: "works well," "is fast," "looks professional," or anything that can't be answered with yes or no.
- I need to be able to check it with my own eyes on screen, without opening code, without installing anything, and without knowing how to code.
- Use concrete, made-up fake data (a name, a phone number, an amount, a date), never "the user enters their data."
- For each good-case criterion, add an ugly-case one: empty field, mistyped data, double click, extremely long text, an accented character, zero units.
- Number them starting from 1. I'll cite those numbers when something fails.

After the list, write a separate section titled THINGS THIS LIST DOESN'T COVER and tell me what's left out, so I can decide whether I care.

Don't write a single line of code in this response.
tasks.expect: Five to eight numbered sentences, all shaped "if I do X, I see Y" with made-up data inside. Plus a final section of what's not covered.
tasks.stuck: If any criterion is still vague ("if I submit the form, it works correctly"), reply: "I can't check criterion 3 just by looking at the screen. Rewrite it with a concrete piece of data and a result I can actually see." Repeat until all eight pass that test.

tasks.title: Ask for the echo before giving the go-ahead
tasks.where: In the same chat, once you have the brief and the checklist.
tasks.action: This is the step everyone skips, and the one that saves the most afternoons. Before it builds anything, ask it to hand your own brief back to you, chewed over. You're going to read what it understood, and that's where the surprises show up. That it assumed you want card payments. That your customers write in another language. That there's a database where there isn't one. Read its answer slowly, line by line. Anything that doesn't match what you had in your head is a badly written piece of your brief, not a failure on its part.
tasks.prompt:
Before building anything, hand my brief back to me, chewed over. Answer with only these four sections and no code:

1. THE BRIEF IN YOUR WORDS: repeat what I asked for in 8 lines max, as if explaining it to someone else who's going to do the work. Don't copy my sentences, rephrase them.

2. WHAT I'M ASSUMING: a list of decisions you're going to make because I never said them. Be suspicious: if you're unsure about something, put it here even if it seems obvious.

3. WHAT'S LEFT FOR ME TO DECIDE: questions you need me to answer. Order them from most result-changing to least, and for each, tell me in one line what happens if I don't answer it.

4. WHAT I'M NOT GOING TO DO: what you've understood to be out of scope for this brief.

If anything in my brief contradicts itself, is impossible, or forces you to make up a fact, tell me now instead of patching it on your own.
tasks.expect: Four sections. The interesting one is #2: a list of assumptions you never wrote. If section 2 is empty or says "none," it hasn't taken this seriously.
tasks.stuck: If section 2 comes back empty, reply: "It's impossible you're not assuming anything. Give me at least five assumptions, even ones that seem obvious." If something in section 1 isn't what you wanted, don't correct it verbally. Go back to your brief, fix the piece that caused it, and ask for the echo again.

tasks.title: Trim the brief down until it fits a five-minute check
tasks.action: You've almost certainly asked for too much at once, and it shows in the list. If it has more than eight criteria, that's several briefs disguised as one. Send the prompt below and keep only the first chunk. It's psychologically hard, because it feels like you're giving up on your idea. You're not: you're splitting it so you can claim it piece by piece. Save the rest in brief.txt under the heading "Next briefs" and don't look at it until this one's done.
tasks.prompt:
Look at my brief and my checklist above. I suspect I've asked for too much at once.

Split it into smaller briefs following this rule: each brief has to be fully checkable in under five minutes and shouldn't carry more than four or five acceptance criteria.

Give me back:
- How many briefs come out of this and each one's title in one line.
- The order they need to happen in and why: what needs what to exist.
- The FIRST one written out in full and ready to work with, with its acceptance criteria numbered and shaped "if I do X, I see Y."
- Which parts of my original brief are decoration and could go undone forever without anything serious happening.

Be tough on me: I'd rather have four boring briefs I can check than one big one I can't.
tasks.expect: A list of three to five briefs with clear titles and an explained order. The first one comes written out in full, with four or five criteria.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you chunks that can't be checked separately (like "brief 1: the internal structure"), reply: "I can't check brief 1 just by looking at the screen. Split it again, and make sure each chunk ends in something I can open and see."

tasks.title: Run the same job twice: the weak sentence and the brief
tasks.where: In two separate new chats, within the same app.
tasks.action: This is the experiment that makes the lesson stick. Open a new chat and paste just your weak sentence from task 1, the one-liner. Wait for the result and don't touch anything. Open another new chat and paste your first trimmed brief with its numbered criteria. Wait for the second result. Now put them side by side and ask yourself one thing only: with which of the two could I say no, pointing at something specific? With the first you can only say "I'm not convinced," which is useless. With the second you can say "criterion 4 fails."
tasks.expect: Two visibly different results. The weak chat's result usually brings things you never asked for (extra sections, made-up copy, prices that don't exist). The brief's result usually brings less and all of it yours.
tasks.stuck: If the weak result looks better because it's flashier, check its details: is your real name in it? Your prices? Your email? Almost always they're pretty and made up. That's exactly the letdown this lesson is about.

tasks.title: Run the list against the result, criterion by criterion, yes or no
tasks.where: With the result open on screen and your brief.txt file next to it.
tasks.action: This is where you stop being the audience. Take criterion 1, literally do what it says, with the exact data it specifies, and write OK or NO next to it. Then #2. Then #3. Don't skip the ugly ones, they're the ones that fail. If a criterion says "I type a 5-digit phone number," type five real digits, not four or seven. Don't trust the AI telling you it meets all six. It hasn't opened your screen or touched anything: it's only rereading what it wrote. Time yourself: if this takes more than five minutes, your brief was too big and next time you cut it sooner.
tasks.expect: Your list with an OK or a NO next to each number. On the NOs, add a short line of what you actually saw instead of what was expected.
tasks.stuck: If you don't know how to test a criterion ("an email arrives at..."), it means the criterion needed something that isn't set up yet. Mark it "not testable yet" and note it for the next brief, instead of accepting it. A criterion you can't check is a criterion that doesn't exist.

tasks.title: Claim only what failed, citing the criterion number
tasks.where: In the chat where you got the good result.
tasks.action: Don't write "this doesn't work" or "fix everything." Write the prompt below, filling in the blanks with your list's numbers and what you actually saw on screen. Citing the number has a strange and very useful effect. The AI stops reinterpreting your brief and focuses on the exact sentence you both agreed on. The "don't touch what already passes" rule stops it from breaking criterion 2 while fixing criterion 4. That's the most common way to lose an afternoon.
tasks.prompt:
I've checked your delivery against my checklist, one by one, on screen. Result:

PASS: [NUMBERS OF THE CRITERIA THAT PASS]

FAIL:
- Criterion [NUMBER]: I did [EXACTLY WHAT YOU DID, WITH THE DATA YOU TYPED] and expected [WHAT THE CRITERION SAID], but what I saw was [WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED].
- Criterion [NUMBER]: I did [...] and expected [...], but what I saw was [...].

Fix only those criteria. Rules:
1. Don't touch anything that already passes. If fixing one requires touching something that already works, tell me BEFORE and wait for my answer.
2. Don't add new features, and don't change text, colors, names, or order I didn't ask for.
3. Give me back the whole file, no trimming and no "...unchanged from here...".
4. When you're done, tell me in one line per criterion exactly what you changed and how I check it on screen.
5. If a criterion can't be met exactly as I wrote it, tell me and explain why in plain language, instead of giving me something close and pretending it's the same.
tasks.expect: A new delivery plus the line pairs from point 4: what got touched and how you check it. You run the whole list again, not just the criteria that failed.
tasks.stuck: If fixing #4 breaks #2, don't argue: write "Fixing criterion 4 broke criterion 2, which was passing before. Revert to the previous version and fix 4 without touching the part that handles 2." And if that happens twice in a row, the brief was too big: split it again.

tasks.title: Save your brief as a template for the rest of the project
tasks.where: In the chat, then in a text file on your Desktop.
tasks.action: All of this gets lost the moment you close the tab. Tomorrow you'll start from zero with an AI that remembers nothing about your project. Ask for the template with the prompt below, copy what it gives you, and paste it into a new file called brief-template.txt on your Desktop. From now on, every time you open a chat for this project, you paste the template and fill in the brackets. You're now briefing in two minutes instead of twenty.
tasks.prompt:
Take everything we've done in this conversation and turn it into a reusable brief template for the rest of my project.

Give it back to me as a single plain-text block I can copy and paste into a file, shaped like this:

- A PROJECT CONTEXT block that never changes: what it is, who uses it, what we've already decided, what parts exist and shouldn't be touched, and how I want you to talk to me (no untranslated technical words, complete files never trimmed, warn me before touching anything that already works).

- A TODAY'S BRIEF block with bracketed blanks I fill in each time: outcome, context, input and output, boundaries, delivery format.

- A HOW I'LL CHECK IT block with the reminder of the "if I do X, I see Y" shape, the rule of adding one ugly case per good case, and numbered blanks for my criteria.

- At the end, three fixed instruction sentences for you that I want repeated in every chat for this project.

Write it exactly as-is, with no explanation before or after. I want to paste it into a file and use it tomorrow without editing it.
tasks.expect: A block of text with four sections and bracketed blanks, no explanations around it. You paste it into brief-template.txt and you now have your way of working.
tasks.stuck: If it comes back full of explanations and comments, reply: "Give me only the template text, no intro or closing, so I can copy it whole." If the context block comes out huge, ask it to keep it to fifteen lines. If it doesn't fit on one screen, you'll never actually paste it.

matters: The sixth piece, the proof. Without it you're not the client, you're the audience. They show you something nice and you clap or stay quiet, but you can't say no while pointing at anything specific. It hurts because you end up accepting work that doesn't hold up and finding out three weeks later, once you've already built five things on top of it.

Writing the checklist BEFORE anything gets built. If you write it afterward, you write it looking at what's already in front of you, and without meaning to, you'll write it to pass. It happens to everyone, it's not a matter of honesty: it's a matter of order.

The ugly case. Almost every failure that's going to ruin your afternoon isn't in the pretty case. It's in the empty field, the five-digit phone number, the accented character, the customer who clicks Submit twice. If you don't ask for it in the brief, it doesn't happen, because nobody asked for it.

Saving the brief in a file of yours, not in the conversation. Chats fill up, get cut off, close by accident, and get forgotten. If your brief only lived there, tomorrow you start from zero. The AI will build you something different, with the exact same confident face as today.
ignore: The names of the techniques: chain of thought, few-shot (with examples), role prompting (giving it a role). These are academic labels for things you're already doing when you write a decent brief. Write good briefs, and the day someone tells you the name, you'll recognize it instantly.

Which model is the best. A well-written brief works well on Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini. A weak one works badly on all three. The difference between models starts showing once the brief is already good, not before.

The paid plan. With the free version of Claude or ChatGPT you can write and check briefs all afternoon. The $20 a month of a paid plan buys you more messages and more powerful models, not better briefs. Pay for it the day you run out of messages mid-task, not before.
canDo: Turn your messy paragraph into the six ordered pieces, if you ask it to interview you instead of solve it for you.
Write your acceptance criteria better than you'd write them yourself. That said: give it the brief first and explicitly ban vague phrases.
Find the gaps you don't see: ask you the five uncomfortable questions that decided the project and that nobody had asked you.
Repeat your own brief back in different words. It's the cheapest way there is to catch a misunderstanding before it costs two hours.
cantDo: It can't actually check its own criteria. It'll tell you "meets all six" with total confidence even if the third one fails. It's rereading what it wrote: it doesn't open your page or type a five-digit phone number. That part is on you, with your own fingers.

It doesn't know what "professional" means in your industry, what price is expensive to your customers, or what word scares them off. If you don't tell it, it'll give you the internet average, which is almost never your case.

It doesn't remember last week's brief. Even if the app has memory, it's not reliable for this: every new chat starts knowing only what you paste into it. That's why the brief lives in your file and not in the conversation.
It won't warn you your brief is weak unless you ask it to. With "make me a website" it won't object: it'll happily start building, and that's exactly where the three lost afternoons begin.
words: The text you type into the AI's box and send all at once, whether it's one sentence or two pages.
A message that, besides asking for something, says what needs to come out and for whom. It also says what shouldn't be touched and how you'll know it's right.
A sentence shaped "if I do this, I see that," answerable only with yes or no. It's what decides whether the work is done or not.

What you put into something and what it gives back. In a booking form, the input is the name and phone number the customer types. The output is the notice they see on screen and the email that reaches you.
How far the work you asked for goes and where it stops. If you don't say so, it stretches on its own and you end up with a blog you never wanted.

The ugly situation nobody tests. For example: the field left blank, the five-digit phone number, or a name with an accented character. Also an order for zero units and a button clicked twice in a row.
Asking for a change, looking at the result, checking it, and asking for the next one. Moving forward in checkable chunks instead of asking for everything at once.
When the AI makes something up with total confidence: a price, an address, a button that doesn't exist. It's not lying to you on purpose, it's filling a gap you left open.
Everything the AI knows about your matter in this specific conversation. Only what you've written in here; nothing more.
next: Take the first trimmed brief and its criteria list, open it in a clean chat, and use it to build the smallest piece of your project that can already be opened, looked at, and checked.
